blocks.body:
Tokenism is including a person as a symbolic effort — to prevent criticism — so the group can look diverse. The invitation is often not about the work. It is about the identity the institution wants to display: race, ethnicity, gender, disability.

A diversity council with no diversity at the table that decides. Hiring without retention. Asking one person to be the voice of the agency when a DEI problem hits the news. targetLesson.title: How we know — and what a gap cannot prove

blocks.alt: Documents on a table — method is how a claim earns the word evidence.
blocks.caption: Bertrand and Mullainathan (2004): identical resumes, names randomized. White-sounding names got significantly more callbacks. That isolates perceived race in one setting. It does not settle a legislature.

blocks.body:
Audit studies randomize a racial signal (a name, an appearance) and hold the rest constant. Clean causal evidence in a narrow market (hiring, housing). Not a picture of a whole life.

Administrative data (wait times, removals, imprisonment) can show large disparities. They rarely isolate a single cause. A gap can be current discrimination, accumulated history, offending, eligibility, or a mix.

Attitude surveys measure what people say they believe. They do not measure what a portal does at 7 p.m.

No single method is decisive. The rigorous move is to triangulate: where independent methods point the same way — housing, lending, hiring — the finding is mainstream, not fringe.

blocks.body: This lesson is not a tour of private stages. It is five DHS surfaces where “the same for everyone” is the design. If you recognize your unit, that is useful. If you do not, take the nearest cousin.
blocks.heading: Stay in the work
In this lesson you will

Tell a legal identical requirement from a lazy identical process.

Mark one surface on the process you named in lesson 1.

blocks.body: A blended average that looks fine can hide the group this change will hit first. That is Minimization with a chart.

tabs.body: One greeting, one ID rule, English-only signage, a portal kiosk with no staffed phone. Fair because identical. Unusable for language, disability, or someone who cannot stand in that line.
tabs.label: Front desk

tabs.body: Statewide wait improved. No race, language, disability, or county breakout. “We don’t have that data” is a finding. Using the blend as proof is Minimization.
tabs.label: Data

tabs.body: The same interview, the same unpaid extra step, the same “culture fit.” Identical. Built for people who already look like the unit.
tabs.label: Hiring

tabs.body: “Families will handle nights” as if every household were the same household. Some are already carrying three jobs. Some are not safe. Some are a Tribal kin network the form cannot see.
tabs.label: Family / unpaid work

tabs.body: Attached after the vote, or filled with “all Minnesotans will benefit.” That is not analysis. That is Minimization wearing the Equity Policy.
tabs.label: The toolkit

blocks.alt: Printed pages on a desk — a chart that may be hiding a group.
blocks.caption: If the packet cannot name a group, it cannot see a disparity. The policy already defined disparity that way.

blocks.feedbackCorrect: Correct. A blend plus a blank form is the habit. Adaptation would break it out and change the path.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: Mentioning a group is not Polarization. A dashboard without a who is Minimization, not proof.

options.text: Average wait is the fairness measure. Ship it.
The blend may hide who got slower. The blank toolkit is sameness-as-process with a cover sheet. Ask for the breakout and a design change before the lock.
Only Equity staff may question a dashboard.
This is Polarization because someone mentioned race.

blocks.alt: The worksheet — the loop has to survive an ordinary packet.
blocks.caption: If the method needs a 40-page binder, the cover sheet will win. Write short, specific lines.

blocks.body: You already did steps 1–3 (results, data, engagement). The rest of the official toolkit is: benefits and burdens plus a design change; a short impact statement; accountability with names and dates; alignment with equity people and policy; sustainability — is this funded and able to collect the data you promised.
blocks.heading: How do you know it is working?
In this lesson
items: Run toolkit steps 4–8 on the same piece of work.
Treat “we will monitor” as not a modification.
Write a statement only this proposal could wear.
Refuse an unfunded mitigation.

blocks.body: A mitigation that lives only in a “we will monitor” sentence is not a modification. Change the design. If it is not funded, write that.

items.body: Who is better off. Who pays in time, money, access, dignity, or risk. What you will change in the design before approval. Does this still match step 1?
items.title: 4. Benefits, burdens, unintended consequences

items.body: Six to ten sentences: action, groups, what data and engagement showed, main benefit, main burden, design change, remaining risk. No slogan.
items.title: 5. Equity impact statement

items.body: Three rows: impact review (who, when); outcome review (who, when); communication (who, when, which audience — including people who carry the burden).
items.title: 6. Accountability

items.body: Sit with the equity director or committee before the freeze. Match equity policy and the strategic plan. Do not bcc after the packet is locked.
items.title: 7. Alignment

items.body: Personnel, money, data collection, engagement. If the phone line in your mitigation has no FTE, you did not mitigate. You wrote fiction.
items.title: 8. Sustainability

blocks.cite: A statement that could only belong to this proposal
blocks.text: We are moving visit requests online. People with disabilities, limited English, and greater-Minnesota households without reliable internet will feel this first. Data shows phone requests are already how those groups reach us. We will keep a staffed phone and in-person path, in plain language and the languages we already fail. The remaining risk is night and weekend coverage — named, dated, and owned.

blocks.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Unfunded mitigation is not mitigation. Change the work or change the date.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: Step 8 is whether it can actually run. A press line is not a phone line.

options.text: Approve and hope a vacancy appears.
Write that the mitigation is unfunded, delay or change the launch until the line is real, and sit with the equity director and the budget owner before Friday.
Put the phone line in “year two” and launch anyway.
Ask Communications to announce both the portal and a future phone line.

blocks.question: The analysis is complete. The mitigation (a staffed phone line) has no budget. Approval is Friday. Strongest move?

items.text: Keep a translated phone path because the burden is already visible.
Six sentences only this proposal could wear.

Impact owner + date; communication owner + audience.
No FTE for the mitigation — delay the launch.

blocks.body: A method is what you do when the meeting is tired. Write the circle so you still ask for a yes.

items.body: Privately first. Family, friends, neighbors, faith, chosen family. Who is in the meeting. Who is not. Do not start with the loudest relative.
items.title: 1. Ask who they want

items.body: A yes with a limit. Sunday rides, not every night. Translation, not the only voice. If they cannot say no in the room, ask again without the audience.
items.title: 2. Ask what they can actually do

items.body: Hours, days, what happens if they are sick. If you cannot write it, it is not a plan. It is a hope.
items.title: 3. Name unpaid work as work

items.body: Paid hours, respite, CFSS/CDCS, a neighbor who said yes on Saturdays with a backup. The gap is staff work, not a moral test for family.
items.title: 4. Fund the gap

items.body: Guardianship, 245D restrictions, maltreatment. Use them. Do not let them become the whole circle.
items.title: 5. Keep legal doors in their lane

items.body: When someone looks exhausted, when a yes changes, when a friend moves. An undated “family will handle it” is a future crisis.
items.title: 6. Review — tired is a finding

blocks.feedbackCorrect: Correct. A no is data. The gap is ours to fund. She can still be family without being the night shift.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: They named a limit. Your job is to fund the gap, not to talk her back into unpaid nights.

options.text: Ask her to try a little longer. The waiver waitlist is long.

Remove her from the person’s life to keep boundaries clean.
Ask the person to convince her in the next team meeting.

blocks.body: A method is what you do when the shift changes. Write the name and the circle so Tuesday-night staff do not invent a briefing.

items.body: Privately, with the device if they need it. Name, pronouns, how to say it. Do not require a speech. Do not correct their word.
items.title: 1. Ask — the name they use

items.body: Which staff, which family, which housemates, which clinic. Different people may get different information. Write it.

items.body: Door, meeting, MAR-as-used, how we call them in the waiting room. Legal name only where the document requires it.

items.body: If the form cannot hold the name, add a line. If the waiting-room script deadnames, change the script. The form is staff work.

items.body: Dating, community, clothes, a partner at the table. Ordinary safety. Not a house announcement.

items.body: When someone is hired, when a family pushes, when they change the circle. An undated “everyone knows” is outing waiting to happen.

blocks.body: Staff need a loop that survives a full caseload. Six moves: ask this week’s energy; put last time on paper; shorten the visit; write the next step in their hands; keep the stacked stories on the page; review when the injury is still changing.
blocks.heading: How do you know it is working?
In this lesson
items: Run the pace-and-write loop on one person you already serve.
Write the next step so it survives the parking lot.
Use questions that do not start with a trap.
Avoid the usual pitfalls: one long meeting, a frozen last year, and a no-show as character.

blocks.body: A method is what you do when the meeting is tired. Write it down so you still offer a short visit and a card in the pocket.

items.body: Open with how the battery is, not with a quiz. Sleep, pain, lights, what already happened this morning. If they have been tested before, say you are not testing them now.
items.title: 1. Ask — this week’s energy

items.body: Do not ask them to perform recall. Show last time. Ask what still fits. Memory is the injury. Paper is the method.
items.title: 2. Put last time on paper

items.body: One or two topics. A visit they can leave with energy left. A long success in the room can be a crash in the car.
items.title: 3. Shorten

items.body: A card, a text they can find, a calendar they actually use. If it only lives in SSIS, it does not live in their week.
items.title: 4. Write the next step in their hands

items.body: Pain, mental health, housing, substance use, another disability. If the plan is only “BI Waiver,” the rest will ambush the week.
items.title: 5. Keep the stack

items.body: A goal can be real. An undated copy of last year is a freeze. Put the next look on the plan. They can still want work. You cannot hide from the calendar.
items.title: 6. Review — the injury is still changing

blocks.alt: Listening with the laptop closed.
blocks.caption: Listening is a control, like a med pass. If it is not on the plan, the pop quiz will win at 10 a.m.

tabs.body: A checkbox that says “goals reviewed.” A quiz. A two-hour meeting. A voicemail they will not recall. Leaders learn about harm from a no-show they cannot explain.
tabs.label: Weak

tabs.body: Energy first, last time on paper, a short visit, a card in the pocket, stacked stories, a dated review.
tabs.label: Strong

tabs.body: A 40-page cognitive profile nobody opens on Saturday. If the method takes longer than the meeting, the quiz will win. Keep it short and mandatory.
tabs.label: Too heavy

blocks.feedbackCorrect: Correct. They named the battery. You have a visit to design. Last month’s face is not this week’s tank.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: They named fatigue. Your job is pace and paper, not a longer meeting and not a pep talk.

options.text: Push through. Looking fine means they can do it.
Thank them, shorten today, put last time on paper, write one next step in their hands, and date a review of length — honor the battery they named.
Cancel all contact to honor the injury.
Ask them to present their limits in the next team meeting.

items.text: Ask how this morning already used their energy.
Leave one next step on a card they take.
Keep housing and pain on the same page as the BI goal.
Cut the visit to 30 minutes.
Show last month’s notes instead of quizzing.

blocks.caption: The method has to survive a Tuesday meeting. If it needs a 40-page sensory binder, the old group will win.

blocks.body: Staff need a loop that survives a full caseload. Not a neurodiversity manual. Six moves: ask how they communicate and what they call themselves; match that in the room; change the environment before the goal; teach only a skill they want; document both columns; review every compliance goal on a dated calendar.
blocks.heading: How do you know it is working?

blocks.body: This lesson is the job-aid underneath the job aid — why each step exists, and what “good enough” looks like.

blocks.heading: In this lesson you will
items: Run the environment-first loop on one person you already serve.
Write the communication, the room, and the skill — not only the face.
Use questions that invite a real yes or a real no.
Avoid the usual pitfalls: one noisy group, a standing social-skills goal, and a frozen “noncompliant.”

blocks.body: A method is what you do when the meeting is tired. Write it down so Tuesday-you still offers a usable room.

items.body: Open with their words and their tools. Device, typing, extra time, a walk while talking. Ask autistic or person with autism. If they have been trained to perform, say you are asking again because the performance is not the person.
items.title: 1. Ask — how they communicate, what they call themselves

items.body: The device in the bag. The interpreter. The extra ten minutes. If you cannot match it today, that is a finding — not “they would not engage.”
items.title: 2. Match communication

items.body: Light, noise, surprise, length, number of voices. The least change that actually works. A quieter offer is a first tool, not a last one.
items.title: 3. Change the room

items.body: A bus. A job. Cooking. Sleep. If the goal is only eye contact, it is our manners. Skill-building is real. Put their destination on the page.
items.title: 4. Teach only what they want

items.body: What they want. What the room did. What communication worked. What compliance goal remains, if any. If a provider in the room sells stillness as easier staffing, write that conflict down too.
items.title: 5. Document — both columns

items.body: A skill goal can be real. An undated “sit still” is a lifestyle. Put the next look on the plan. The person can still want a skill. You cannot hide from the calendar.
items.title: 6. Review — the compliance goal has a date

blocks.alt: Listening with the laptop closed.
blocks.caption: Listening is a control, like a med pass. If it is not on the plan, the old group will win at 10 a.m.

blocks.body: You do not need a perfect neurodiversity plan to start. You need a door: “Here is how you communicate. Here is what we changed in the room. Here is the skill you asked for. Here is any compliance goal and when we will look at it again. Here is how you say stop.” Then mean it.
blocks.heading: A usable status line

tabs.body: A checkbox that says “communication discussed.” A group they cannot stand. A social-skills goal copied from last year. Leaders learn about harm from a licensing visit they cannot explain.
tabs.label: Weak

tabs.body: Their words first, the device in the room, the lights named, a skill they asked for, both columns written, a dated review.
tabs.label: Strong

tabs.body: A 40-page sensory profile nobody opens on Saturday. If the method takes longer than the meeting, the old group will win. Keep it short and mandatory.
tabs.label: Too heavy

cards.back: If “they had a behavior” is the whole story, you have not looked. Specific environment gets specific change.
cards.front: Name the room in one sentence

cards.back: Planning without their words is staff planning. Access is part of step 1.
Do not cheer only stillness. A documented stop that we honor is success of process. A coerced group is a later crisis.
cards.front: Protect the yes and the stop

cards.back: If you cannot write a review date, you are not ready to train the face. You are ready to hope no one asks.

blocks.feedbackCorrect: Correct. They named an environment. You have a life to design. The sentence they gave you is data, not a closed file and not a void.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: They named a room that does not work. Your job is environment design, not a social-skills override and not a pep talk.

options.text: Refuse. Group is how we socialize people.
Thank them, name the noise, offer a quieter way to get the same life (a job, a club, a walk), write both columns, and date any remaining group goal — honor stop as far as the real need allows.
Cancel all community to honor neurodiversity.
Ask them to present their feelings in the next team meeting.

blocks.question: A person says, “I don’t want group.” They stim and leave noisy rooms. Best next step?

blocks.body: The hardest part is not the loop. It is delaying a convenient group until the person has a usable hour. That pause is neurodiversity. Installing the old group on time is not.

items.body: Ask how they talk, what they call themselves, and wait. A shy yes after a power meeting is not a reliable sample.
items.title: Pitfall: “Any communication needs?” as the whole offer

items.body: Write the review date into the plan. Memory is not a control.
items.title: Pitfall: “We’ll remember next quarter.”

items.body: If the conversation is unusable, there was no conversation. Devices, extra time, and a quieter room are part of step 1.
items.title: Pitfall: treating the device as a later translation

items.body: “Before we keep this social-skills goal — have we named their words, the room, the skill they want, and the date?” That sentence changes more behavior than a branded campaign.
items.title: Better: close in the room

items.text: Ask whether they say autistic or person with autism.
Dim the lights and allow headphones.
Write the social-skills goal and a review date on the same page.
Teach bus riding because they asked for it.
Bring the tablet instead of “working on talking.”

blocks.alt: A latched kitchen door in a residential hallway.
blocks.caption: Restrict-to-protect ends at the latch. Support-to-live designs the hour after you open it.

blocks.body: Teams get stuck in a false choice: either we lock everything, or we ignore risk and call it dignity. Health, wellness, and safety are neither. Some restrictions are medically required and time-limited. Some are the team’s anxiety with a form attached. Support-to-live names the real risk and puts a person next to it. Restrict-to-protect names our fear and puts a door in front of it.
blocks.heading: Why the debate matters

blocks.body: This lesson compares those frames so you can pick the right one — without using “they’ll get hurt” as a way to skip a life you still owe.

blocks.heading: In this lesson
items: Tell a real restriction from a house rule with letterhead.
Keep support real when a guardian or a prior incident is loud.
Hold trauma without making protocol the next injury.
Know when maltreatment, licensing, or consultation leave the huddle.

blocks.body: A hard medical risk does not cancel the life. It changes the support. A real restriction still requires a date.

items.body: Lead with the worst day. Lock, cancel, delay. Fast in the meeting. Slow across a life. Use a restriction when the risk is real and the support is not yet in place. Do not use it as the plan forever.
items.title: Restrict-to-protect

items.body: The life is on the table first. The risk is named in plain language. Support stands next to the stove, the sidewalk, the clinic. You will still have incidents. That is not the same as designing a cage.
items.title: Support-to-live

items.body: Maltreatment, a 245D rights restriction process, a physician order, emergency hold, and Tribal consultation are not informal team judgments. Use the proper door. Do not workshop a duty that belongs to licensing, a clinician, or a government-to-government path.
items.title: Formal path — when the huddle is the wrong room

blocks.alt: Two people walking and talking on a Minnesota park path.
blocks.caption: Support-to-live is visible: they are outside. Someone is with them. The risk was not imaginary. It was designed around.

blocks.body: If you only watch for incidents, you will miss a person who wanted a walk. If you only watch for choice, you may miss a medical risk you are required to name. If you only watch for the people already closest to the default, you will call the rest unsafe.
blocks.heading: Frameworks shape what you notice

tabs.body: An adult wants to walk to the store. They have gotten lost before. The guardian is afraid. Staffing is thin on Saturdays. They use a communication device.
tabs.label: The issue

tabs.body: No store. “Too risky.” The device stays home. Fear wins because it was the only expert in the room.
tabs.label: Restrict-to-protect

tabs.body: Device comes. A staff person walks with them, then a fade toward more independence. A simple check-in plan. Guardian is in the conversation, not the only voice. Review date on any extra support.
tabs.label: Support-to-live

tabs.body: If a rights restriction is actually being used, use the 245D process. If maltreatment is suspected, report. If a Tribal program is involved, ask consultation leads. Do not “engage” your way around those doors.
tabs.label: Formal path

cards.back: Should make a life possible. If the only outcome is “stay home,” it is a restriction with better branding.
Needs information, experience, and a chance to try. A no from a guardian is not the same as the person’s informed no.
The smallest support that actually works. A lock on the whole house is rarely the least. A person at the stove often is.
Not “be nicer.” It is: no surprise, no extra force, predictable people, the device in the room, a way to say stop that we will honor.

blocks.feedbackCorrect: Correct. History is data for support design. It is not a lifetime stay-home order.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: Do not erase the incident. Do not let it freeze a life. Design around the actual risk.

options.text: Agree. Prior incidents cancel community life.
Ignore the incident and send them alone this afternoon.
Name the real getting-lost risk, put community time on the page with support and the device, and date a review — do not let two-year-old fear run the calendar.
Write “family declined” and close the wellness goal.

blocks.question: A supervisor says, “We had a missing-person incident two years ago, so community time is off the table.” What is the strongest response?

blocks.body: Teams disagree about how fast to fade a support, how much risk a guardian will allow, and when a medical order is truly required. Disagreement about pacing is allowed. Never offering the sidewalk, because it would be uncomfortable, is not a professional debate.
blocks.heading: Where people of good faith disagree
Real disagreements — and the line they may not cross

items.body: If you cannot name a date, it is already a lifestyle. Put the date on the plan. The person can still need the support. They cannot get free of a restriction you never reopen.
items.title: How soon to review a restriction?

items.body: A social story is not community experience. A supported outing is closer to informed choice than a brochure about “staying safe.”
items.title: When is a try enough?

items.body: The person, after information, with supported decision-making if needed. Not the loudest night supervisor, and not the lock we already installed. Write what they want, what we tried, and what restriction remains — with a date.
items.title: Who decides it is good enough?

blocks.body: Fact: people cannot choose a walk they were never offered. Prescription: whether you use a supported outing, a fade plan, or a clinic with an interpreter this month. Argue about the prescription. Do not argue about the fact.
blocks.heading: Facts versus prescriptions

items.text: Walk to the store with staff and the communication device.
Cancel all outings because of a two-year-old incident.
Report suspected maltreatment instead of “handling it in-house.”
Assume a Tribal citizen will not want community food practices.
Use the 245D process if you are actually restricting a right.

blocks.body: Staff need a loop that survives a full caseload. Not a 40-page employment manual. Six moves: ask about work first; try work in the community; name the money and the fear; connect to Engage / Plan / Find / Keep and the right partners; document the choice without a conflict of interest; review the no on a dated calendar.
blocks.heading: How do you know it is working?

blocks.body: This lesson is the job-aid underneath the job aid — why each step exists, and what “good enough” looks like.

blocks.heading: In this lesson
items: Run the first-option loop on one person you already serve.
Write what they want, what they fear, and what they tried.
Use questions that invite a real yes or a real no.
Avoid the usual pitfalls: one mention, a brochure, and a frozen no.

blocks.body: A method is what you do when the meeting is tired. Write it down so you still offer work first.

items.body: Open with work. “What kind of work interests you?” not “We have a Monday opening.” If they have said no before, say you are asking again because the offer stands.
items.title: 1. Ask — work before the other slot

items.body: A brochure is not experience. A visit, a short tryout, a conversation with a worker who does the job. Discovery and job carving belong here for people who will not fit a posted listing.
items.title: 2. Community experience — not only on paper

items.body: Say that work can change benefits, and that a planner can show the numbers. Point to DB101 and Disability Hub. Do not give hallway tax advice. Do not let a rumor close the file.
items.title: 3. Name the money — benefits and wage

items.body: Match the phase. Curious but not sure: Engage. Ready to design a path: Plan. Looking: Find, including VR and employment services. Hired: Keep, including natural supports and transportation. Do not dump everyone into Find.
items.title: 4. Connect — Engage, Plan, Find, Keep

items.body: What they heard. What they tried. What they chose. Why, in their words if you can. If a provider in the room sells the alternative service, write that conflict down too.
items.title: 5. Document — the person’s choice, not the team’s relief

items.body: A no is allowed. An undated no is a sideline. Put the next ask on the plan. The person can stop you. You cannot stop yourselves from offering.
items.title: 6. Review — the no has a date

blocks.alt: An employment specialist listening with the laptop closed.
blocks.caption: Listening is a control, like an authorization or a start date. If it is not on the plan, the default will win.

blocks.body: You do not need a perfect employment plan to start. You need a door: “Work is the first option. Here is what we know about what you want, what we don’t know about benefits, and when we’ll know more. Here is who can help. Here is how you say no without disappearing from the next review.” Then mean it.
blocks.heading: A usable status line

tabs.body: A checkbox that says “employment discussed.” A flyer. A no copied from last year. Questions go to a generic inbox. Leaders learn about under-employment from a dashboard they cannot explain.
tabs.label: Weak

tabs.body: Work first on the agenda, a community experience, a benefits appointment, a named phase in Engage / Plan / Find / Keep, a written choice, a dated review.
tabs.label: Strong

tabs.body: A 40-page career binder nobody opens. If the method takes longer than the meeting, the open slot will win. Keep it short and mandatory.
tabs.label: Too heavy

cards.back: Engage, Plan, Find, or Keep. If “the team” owns employment, no one does.
Benefits, transportation, failure, family. Unnamed fear writes the plan in invisible ink.
Do not cheer only the yes. A documented no after a real offer is success of process. A coerced yes is a later crisis.
cards.front: Protect the yes and the no

cards.back: If you fill the day-program slot first, you are choosing. Write that you chose. Better: pause the slot until the offer is real.

blocks.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Fear plus facts. The sentence they gave you is data, not a closed file.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: They named the classic barrier. Your job is a planner, not a rumor and not a pep talk.

options.text: Agree that work is too risky and close employment.
Thank them, name the fear as legitimate, book benefits counseling / DB101 support, and keep work on the table until they have numbers — then document their choice.
Tell them most people are fine and they should try anyway this week.
Ask them to present their feelings in the next team meeting.

blocks.question: A person says, “I don’t want to lose my benefits.” Best next step?

blocks.body: The hardest part is not the loop. It is delaying a convenient slot until the person has heard a real offer. That pause is Employment First. Filling the slot on time is not.

items.body: Ask what kind of work, who they already know, what a good day looks like, and wait. A shy no after a power meeting is not a reliable sample.
items.title: Pitfall: “Any interest in work?” as the whole offer

items.body: Write the review date into the plan. Memory is not a control.
items.title: Pitfall: “We’ll remember next year.”

items.body: If the offer is unusable, there was no offer. Interpreters, captions, and plain language are part of step 1, not a sequel.
items.title: Pitfall: treating access as a later translation

items.body: “Before we fill another service — have we offered work, named benefits, and written the choice?” That sentence changes more behavior than a branded campaign.
items.title: Better: close in the room

items.text: Open the meeting with the job question before the day-program slot.
Book a benefits counseling appointment.
Write the person’s no in their words and set a review date.
Match them to Find and make a VR referral.
A community tryout at a real workplace.

blocks.caption: The method fits on one page. If it needs a binder, it will not be used on a busy day.

blocks.body: Leaders need a loop that survives a busy week. Not a 40-page change-management plan. Six moves: name what is changing and what is ending; invite the people who will live with it while the design can move; sequence who knows before the public; listen to resistance as data; close the loop in writing; repair without making the messenger do your guilt work.
blocks.heading: How do you know it is working?

blocks.body: This lesson is the job-aid underneath the job aid — why each step exists, and what “good enough” looks like.

blocks.heading: In this lesson
items: Run the along-loop on a change you already own.
Write a know / don’t know / when we’ll know note.
Use questions that invite holes in the plan.
Avoid the usual pitfalls: fake influence, one email, and punishing candor.

blocks.body: A method is what you do when you are tired. Write it down so you can still lead on a busy day.

items.body: One page: what will be different on a named date, what stops, who is affected, what is not changing. If you cannot say what ends, people will keep both worlds running.
items.title: 1. Name — the work and the ending

items.body: Put the Monday-morning roles in the draft. Say what they can still change. If they can change nothing, do not call it a workshop. Call it a briefing and be decent about it.
items.title: 2. Invite — while it can still move

items.body: Supervisors, public-facing staff, partners, then notices. Book access: captions, interpreters, plain language, time. A change meeting some people cannot use is a decision to exclude.
items.title: 3. Sequence — who acts before the public

items.body: “What will break if we do this as written?” is a better prompt than “any questions?” Write down what you hear. If you will not change it, say why. Silence after a big news is not a vote of confidence.
items.title: 4. Listen — resistance as data

items.body: What we heard. What we changed. What we will not change and why. Who owns questions. When the next update comes, even if the next update is “nothing new.”
items.title: 5. Close — the loop in writing

items.body: You will miss. Name it, restore comparable information the same day, change the checklist, and do not make the person who was left out lead the sharing circle.
items.title: 6. Repair — without theater

blocks.alt: A supervisor listening with the laptop closed.
blocks.caption: Listening is a control, like a date or a budget. If it is not on the plan, it will not happen.

blocks.body: You do not need a perfect comms plan to start. You need a door: “Here is what we know, what we don’t, and when we’ll know more. Here is what you can still influence. Here is how to tell us what will break.” Then mean it.
blocks.heading: A usable status line

tabs.body: A slide deck, a go-live party, a training roster. Questions go to a generic inbox. Leaders learn about holes from the press or from a county board.
tabs.label: Weak

tabs.body: One page, named owner, Monday-morning roles in the draft, a sequence that beats the public letter, a written close-the-loop note, a repair within a day of a miss.
tabs.label: Strong

tabs.body: A 40-page change-management plan nobody opens. If the method takes longer than the change, it will not be used. Keep it short and mandatory.
tabs.label: Too heavy

cards.back: Someone with enough authority to change the design or to tell the truth when it cannot change. If “the project” owns it, no one does.
Inventing certainty is how you bounce later. A dated “we don’t know yet” is adult. A fake FAQ is not.
Thank the person who names a hole in front of other people. If you wince, the next hole arrives as a crisis.
New work without stopped work is a staffing decision you did not admit. Name what comes off the plate, even if the answer is overtime you will actually pay.

blocks.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Data plus dignity. The quiet room was already a finding.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: They gave you a hole in the plan and a fear about punishment. Both are your problem to handle without making them the show.

options.text: Tell them the decision is made so we need positivity now.

Thank them, bring the counter failure into the open without exposing them if they asked for privacy, test the step with people who do the work, and close the loop on what you changed or why you will not.
Forward the email to the whole team as a coaching moment.
Ask them to present their feelings in the next all-staff.

blocks.question: Staff are quiet after you announce a process change. One person emails later: “This will fail at the counter, but I don’t want to be the difficult one.” Best next step?

blocks.body: The hardest part is not the loop. It is delaying a date when the people who must act are not ready. That pause is leadership. Shipping an unusable change on time is not.

items.body: Ask “what will break?” and wait. Count to ten. Questions after a power announcement are not a reliable sample.
items.title: Pitfall: “Any questions?” as the whole engagement

items.body: Write the miss into the one-pager. Memory is not a control.
items.title: Pitfall: “We’ll remember next time.”

items.body: If the change notice is unusable, the change did not reach people. Captions, plain language, and interpreters are part of the sequence, not a sequel.
items.title: Pitfall: treating access as a later translation

items.body: “Before we lock this — who is not here who will live with it, and what will break?” That sentence changes more behavior than a branded campaign.
items.title: Better: close in the room

items.text: Write what stops on the go-live date.
Brief public-facing staff before the client letter is mailed.
Send “what we heard, what we changed, what we won’t.”
A county partner was left off the draft; you call the same day and add their cut.
Ask “what will break?” and wait through the silence.

blocks.caption: Most access work happens before the meeting starts. The empty chair with clear space is a decision.

blocks.body: Leaders do not need a new personality. They need a new default. Four ordinary controls decide whether people can participate: time, tools, talk, and team. If those four are right, many accommodation requests never have to become emergencies.
blocks.heading: What the work actually shows

blocks.body: This lesson is the evidence of practice — what happens when those doors are open, and what people experience when they are not.

blocks.heading: In this lesson
items: Use the four doors as a planning scan before you convene work.
Separate universal design from one-person fixes.
See how language access and disability access travel together.
Name the harm of last-minute materials and uncaptioned video.

blocks.body: Access problems are usually design problems that arrived wearing a calendar.

blocks.heading: The four doors, in operational language

items.body: Interpreters, captioners, reviewers, and people who read slowly or use assistive technology need clock time. Sending a 40-page packet at 8:00 a.m. for a 9:00 a.m. decision is an access denial dressed as urgency. Build lead time into the project plan. Urgency is sometimes real. It is also sometimes a habit.
items.title: Time

items.body: Rooms, platforms, documents, forms, and equipment. Keyboard access, readable PDFs, automatic captions plus a human check, microphones that actually work, hybrid setups that show the same content to everyone. A tool that only some staff can use is a team split.
items.title: Tools

items.body: Effective communication: ASL, captioning, plain language, spoken-language interpreters, large print, and time to process. Talk also means whose voice is invited. If only the fastest speakers in English get heard, the meeting has a design.
items.title: Talk

items.body: Do people with disabilities, and people who use other languages, belong here without penalty? Team is the culture door: no eye-rolls at accommodations, no “gotcha” about attendance at inaccessible events, no promotion path that requires unpaid extra labor to translate the work for yourself.
items.title: Team

blocks.alt: Supervisor and staff member at a public counter working with an interpreter and a member of the public.
blocks.caption: When talk is resourced, the public does not have to bring their own access to a state counter.

blocks.body: Last-minute work does not only stress people. It systematically excludes interpreters, captioners, people who use screen readers on long PDFs, and anyone who cannot drop family care to decode a surprise meeting. If your unit lives in last-minute, you have an access method. It is a harmful one.
blocks.heading: Mechanism: last-minute is a method

cards.back: Deaf and hard-of-hearing staff cannot take part in the live conversation. They get a summary later, which is not the same job.
Screen-reader users hear nothing useful. They must ask for help or skip the decision. The file looks finished. It is not.
Households with limited English proficiency never received the notice. Outreach numbers then look like “low interest.”
Staff stop asking. Needs go underground. That is how you lose people without a resignation letter that says “access.”

blocks.heading: Reading the same meeting three ways

tabs.body: “Did anyone file a request?” If no, proceed. This misses people who do not feel safe asking, and it treats the law as a complaint system instead of a design standard.
tabs.label: Compliance only

tabs.body: “What would make this usable for more people without a special ask?” Captions, plain language, advance materials, a working mic, a hybrid view that matches the room.
tabs.label: Universal design

tabs.body: “What does this person need that the default still does not provide?” A specific interpreter, a different schedule, an alternate format. Still required. Easier when the default is already strong.
tabs.label: Individual accommodation

blocks.feedbackCorrect: Correct. The calendar is a design choice. If the market cannot produce interpreters in 10 days, the date is the barrier.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: A later summary is not the town hall. Interpreter lead time is a known constraint. Leaders plan dates around it the same way they plan around a commissioner’s calendar.

options.text: Cancel language access; 10 days is too short to be required.
Keep the date and offer a written summary afterward.
Time is the blocked door. Move the date, or narrow the event to a format you can make usable — and start interpreter and caption booking as part of setting any new date.
Tools are the only issue; switch to a longer slide template.

blocks.question: A county partner town hall is scheduled in 10 days. The slide deck is not done. Interpreters need more than 10 days in this market. What does the four-doors scan tell you?

blocks.body: When participation is low among people with disabilities or people who speak languages other than English, do not start with “they are hard to reach.” Start with the four doors. You will often find a time, tool, talk, or team problem you already control.
blocks.heading: From observation to explanation
How to check your own unit without a research project

items.body: Were materials on time? Were captions on? Could someone join by phone and still follow? Who spoke? Who left early? That is data.
items.title: Look at the last five meetings

items.body: Run a heading structure check. Try the file with keyboard only. Ask: would this survive a screen reader? If you cannot tell, that is already a finding.
items.title: Look at one document

items.body: Did the posting say how to request accommodation? Did the interview need a surprise video platform? Did the schedule assume one kind of body and brain?
items.title: Look at one hiring loop

items.body: A four-door scan will not replace an investigation or a formal accessibility audit. It will stop you from waiting for a complaint to notice the obvious.
items.title: Limits of this scan

items.text: The packet arrived 20 minutes before a decision meeting.
The hybrid call shows a ceiling mic and no slides to remote staff.
No interpreter was booked for a required public hearing.
A supervisor sighs when a staff member mentions a medical appointment tied to disability.
The “accessible PDF” is a photographed printout.

options.label: Time: move the date or narrow the event to a format everyone can use.
options.response: Correct. Lead time is part of access planning. The calendar is a design decision, not a neutral constraint.

options.label: Tools: buy a longer slide template and keep the date.
options.response: A better template will not solve a deadline that excludes interpreters, captioners, or people who need processing time.

options.response: Waiting transfers the burden to the people already facing the barrier. Scan the four doors before the invite.

U.S. Census Bureau: date the vintage. 2020 Census: about 331 million residents. Race and Hispanic origin are administrative categories — they are not culture. Non-Hispanic White remains the largest single category and is no longer the unmarked future of every county. Hispanic/Latino origin is an ethnicity in Census terms; people still live it as culture. Black, Asian, American Indian and Alaska Native, Native Hawaiian and Other Pacific Islander, and Two or More Races are the other federal race boxes. Date any percentage you put in a report. This page is not a “white culture share.”

Minnesota objects

Minnesota Compass cultural-community profiles are Minnesota objects. They belong on people pages. This umbrella does not replace them.

A rate is not the person.

Date the vintage

Date 2020 Census and later ACS when you write a number into a report. About 331 million in 2020. Hispanic origin ~19% (ethnicity, any race). Black alone ~13–14% depending on vintage and “alone or in combination.” Asian the fastest-growing large category in many metros. American Indian and Alaska Native counts jump when “in combination” is used — Compass Minnesota Native American ~162,216 (ACS 2019–2023) is a Minnesota object, not this page.

Foreign-born share nationally is on the order of 14% in recent ACS vintages — date it. Minnesota’s foreign-born share is lower than some coastal states and still remade whole neighborhoods and plant towns. Language other than English at home: on the order of one in five nationally; Minnesota State Demographic Center cited 11.7% of Minnesotans age 5+ in 2018. Date it. CLAS exists because that 11.7% is not a rounding error at the desk.

Public doors

Census; founding documents; National Archives; Pew on religion; people-page organizations.

Learn on your own time. A colleague is not an unpaid American-culture tutor. Open Minnesota culture.

Read with this page

Read with this page, not instead of it: Tocqueville, Democracy in America (selected); Bellah et al., Habits of the Heart; Takaki, A Different Mirror; Du Bois, The Souls of Black Folk (American and Negro); King, “I Have a Dream” and “Letter from Birmingham Jail”; the 1964 Civil Rights Act as a text; Pew Religious Landscape (date the wave). Then stop reading and open Minnesota culture. Then a people page. Then Tuesday.

blocks.body:
Minnesota Nice is the heart of this brief. Reserved warmth: you will be helped, you may not be hugged. Conflict-avoidance: disagreement goes sideways, into process, into “let’s take this offline,” into silence. Sameness-as-fairness: identical treatment is the moral high ground; a targeted channel looks like playing favorites. Competence as love: we show care by being good at the work, on time, prepared — not by heat. Don’t make a scene. The no that sounds like a yes. “That’s interesting.” “I’ll have to think about it.” “Ope.” “Not too bad.”

What Nice oils, and what it hides

This hymn is real. It oils a dense civic life: cooperatives, volunteering, high turnout, public institutions that often work. It also hides harm. A raised voice from a Black parent is unprofessional. A Somali mother’s directness is rude. A tribal chair who will not smile through a bad consult is difficult. Staff of color learn the weather on day one. Dominant-culture staff call it decent.

Nice is not kindness as such. Kindness can be direct. Nice is a regulation of affect. Intercultural work that never names this regulation will treat every other affect as excess.

Why it frames the work

The form, the hearing, the hiring panel, the “we treat everyone the same” sit inside this hymn. Name it in the room. Mockery does not help. Letting it write the cap as just being adult does not help either.
blocks.heading: Heart of the Culture — Minnesota Nice

blocks.body:
Minnesota Nice — see Heart. The operating system.

Lutheran-civic residue

Even among Catholics, evangelicals, Muslims, and the unaffiliated: suspicion of display, duty, committees, the sermon as civic speech, Jantelagen-adjacent “don’t think you’re special.” Not every Minnesotan is Lutheran. The civic air still tastes like it.

Lake and winter

Recreation as identity for some. Winter as a moral test (“we don’t complain”). Neither is a personality for a waiver household that cannot start a car.

Education as civic religion

Louder than the American average. We are the state that ranks itself. Achievement gaps the state publishes on itself sit next to that pride. Hold both.

Progressive self-image

We vote, we volunteer, we are not Mississippi. Some of the widest racial disparities in the United States in income, homeownership, and criminal-legal contact — date MDH, Compass, and Council on Crime and Justice figures when you cite them. The gap is Minnesota. Nice without the gap is a lullaby.

Equal process

The American sameness-as-fairness concept, intensified. Equity as targeted channel will be felt as unfair until you can say it in this hymn’s language: universal goal, different door, same dignity.

Conflict-avoidance as governance

Meetings without a decision. Consensus as delay. Nation-to-nation consult that is actually a presentation. Ask: what did we decide? Who will do it by when?

Understatement

Boast is a crime. Direct praise can embarrass. Direct criticism can end a relationship. The work is being plain without performing a coastal confrontation style.

You work with these. You do not perform a hotdish.

blocks.body:
Minnesota’s African American population is modest in absolute terms — about 350,000 Black Minnesotans as of 2024, or about 6 percent of the state — and culturally significant and historically deep.

Places

Minneapolis — especially North Minneapolis (the Near North side: Hawthorne, Jordan, Near North, Willard-Hay, Sumner-Glenwood, Harrison), the Black cultural and demographic heart of Minneapolis since the 1910s. MNopedia: the Near North community “has had a major African American presence since the early 1900s.”

South Minneapolis — historically a smaller Black community; Bryant, Bryn Mawr, Field-Regina-Northrop, Powderhorn, Phillips, and Central have all had significant Black populations. The murder of George Floyd at 38th and Chicago in May 2020 put South Minneapolis at the global epicenter of racial justice consciousness.

St. Paul — Rondo was the historic Black community of St. Paul, destroyed by I-94 construction in the 1960s — a generational trauma Black St. Paul still commemorates annually with Rondo Days (the third Saturday of July). Frogtown, Summit-University, and Dayton’s Bluff continue to have significant Black populations.

Brooklyn Park, Brooklyn Center, Robbinsdale, Crystal, New Hope — rapidly diversifying first-ring northwest suburbs, now home to large and growing Black communities, both African American and East African. Eden Prairie, Plymouth, Maple Grove — outer-ring suburbs with growing Black middle-class populations. Duluth, St. Cloud, Rochester — smaller but distinct Black communities, often university or healthcare related.

Minnesota’s Black history includes

Dred and Harriett Scott — enslaved by Dr. John Emerson at Fort Snelling (1830s–1840s); Dred Scott v. Sandford (1857) was a critical step toward the Civil War.

Roy Wilkins — born in St. Louis, raised in St. Paul; long-time executive secretary of the NAACP.

Lena O. Smith — Minnesota’s first Black female attorney (1921); civil rights pioneer.

Nellie Stone Johnson — labor and civil rights leader; first Black person elected to a city office in Minneapolis (1945).

Prince Rogers Nelson — born in North Minneapolis, 1958; one of the greatest musicians in American history.

August Wilson — playwright, raised in Pittsburgh, spent significant years in St. Paul; two Pulitzer Prizes.

Sharon Sayles Belton — first Black woman mayor of Minneapolis (1994–2001). Melvin Carter III — first Black mayor of St. Paul (2018–present). Andrea Jenkins — first openly transgender Black woman elected to public office in the United States (Minneapolis City Council). Keith Ellison — Minnesota Attorney General; first Muslim elected to Congress (2007); prosecuted the George Floyd case. Toni Carter, Rena Moran, and other contemporary African American political leaders. East African Minnesotans in public office, including Ilhan Omar, have their own community pages; shared race in the United States is not shared culture.

Walter “Fritz” Mondale and Hubert Humphrey — white Minnesota political leaders whose civil-rights advocacy was profoundly shaped by Black Minnesota organizing.

The 2020 murder of George Floyd by Minneapolis police, the subsequent uprising, and the global Black Lives Matter mobilization centered Minnesota in American racial discourse. Minnesota’s racial story is now globally known. The state’s African American community navigates both the legacy of the Migration generation and the weight of being where Floyd died.
blocks.heading: Minnesota and African American History

blocks.body:
W.E.B. Du Bois, the foundational African American sociologist and intellectual (1868–1963), wrote in The Souls of Black Folk (1903):

“The history of the American Negro is the history of this strife — this longing to attain self-conscious manhood, to merge his double self into a better and truer self. In this merging he wishes neither of the older selves to be lost. He would not Africanize America, for America has too much to teach the world and Africa. He would not bleach his Negro soul in a flood of white Americanism, for he knows that Negro blood has a message for the world. He simply wishes to make it possible for a man to be both a Negro and an American.”

Double consciousness

Being both Black and American — sharing in the American story while standing outside the dominant white narrative of it — is foundational to African American identity. Understanding African American culture means understanding this double consciousness: the ongoing tension and synthesis between full participation in American life and the maintenance of a distinct, valued, deeply rooted Black cultural identity.

Not one life

What follows is a generalization. Individual variation always supersedes it. Diversity within Black America — across region, class, age, education, religion, sexuality, generation, urban and rural, political orientation — is vast. Always defer to the person in front of you.
blocks.heading: The Heart of the People

blocks.body:
These concepts and values recur across African American culture. They express themselves differently across regions, classes, religious communities, generations, and individual circumstances. They are hypotheses — not a script for the person in front of you.

Blackness

To be Black in America is to live in a culture where racial identity has been a central organizing fact of social existence since 1619. Blackness is at once a racial ascription imposed by a society that categorized people of African descent as “other”; a self-claimed identity affirmed through Black is Beautiful (1960s), natural hair, African heritage, and distinct cultural forms; a political solidarity that crosses class, region, religion, and generation; and a cultural inheritance of music, language, food, religion, family, art, sport, and intellectual tradition.

Blackness is not monolithic, and it is shared. African Americans of all classes, regions, and walks of life recognize each other across difference through the Black nod — the silent acknowledgment between Black strangers in white spaces — the shared vocabulary of references, the common touchstones of Black history.

The race

Older Black Americans, especially those raised before the 1970s, often refer to “the race” — Black people collectively. The usage carries a Du Boisian sense of collective consciousness: that one is responsible to and for the race, that individual successes and failures matter to the race, that one carries the race into white spaces. Racial uplift, sometimes called the “talented tenth” mentality after Du Bois’s controversial term for the educated Black leadership class, shapes much Black middle-class life: “making the race look good,” “representing,” “lifting as we climb” (the motto of the National Association of Colored Women, 1896).

Soul

Soul is one of the most important and least translatable Black cultural concepts. Coined in the 1960s but reflecting a much older sensibility, soul names distinctive emotional depth, expressive authenticity, communal feeling, and spiritual resonance. Soul food, soul music, soul brother / soul sister, having soul — the concept pervades Black self-description. To have soul is to be authentic, to feel deeply, to express truthfully, to be in genuine connection with the community and the ancestors. To lack soul is to be cold, fake, disconnected, or assimilated past recognition.

Respect

Respect is among the most important values in Black social life. To be disrespected — by police, employers, teachers, strangers, family — is a foundational injury. Respect is earned and also fundamentally owed: every human being deserves baseline respect for their personhood. “Respect my Black” names the demand for acknowledgment of full humanity.

Interpersonal respect is signaled through titles and last name (Mr. Johnson, Mrs. Brown, Sister, Brother) until invited otherwise; listening when elders speak; acknowledging people’s presence; not embarrassing people in public; honoring lineage. Aretha Franklin’s “Respect” (1967) became an anthem because it articulated this demand.

Ubuntu

W.E.B. Du Bois devoted considerable time to cooperative economics, an approach rooted in African traditions such as ubuntu — often translated as “I am, because we are.” African American thinkers have embraced the South African / Bantu concept as articulating a sensibility that runs through Black American life: individual flourishing through collective flourishing.

Making a way out of no way

A foundational Black American expression — the recognition that African Americans have survived and even thrived through 400 years of conditions designed to destroy them. The capacity to endure, adapt, improvise, and find joy in hardship is celebrated as a core cultural strength. Black resilience is not stoic suffering but creative survival — making something out of nothing, turning pain into art, dancing at the funeral, laughing through the storm. The Black church song “We’ve Come This Far by Faith” captures it: faith as lived practice of getting through what should not have been gotten through.

Black Excellence

A term that crystallized in the 2010s but expresses a much older sensibility — the celebration of Black achievement in fields where systemic barriers have made achievement extraordinarily hard. It is not assimilationist. It is affirmative: look what we have done despite everything. Invoked at graduations, weddings, professional milestones, and communal — our excellence, not just mine.

Code-switching

The practice of shifting language, demeanor, accent, and presentation between Black and non-Black spaces is a near-universal experience for Black Americans navigating predominantly white institutions. It can mean speaking African American Vernacular English at home and Standard American English at work; wearing professional hair in white workspaces and natural hair at home; adjusting humor, references, tone, volume, body language. It is a survival skill, an art form, and often a source of fatigue. Younger generations increasingly resist it, asserting the right to show up as fully Black in all spaces.

The hustle

Entrepreneurial, multi-job, side-business resourcefulness is a recognized cultural pattern, rooted in centuries of exclusion from mainstream employment and capital. Hustle culture is celebrated in hip-hop. The concept honors economic creativity born of necessity.

Sankofa

The Akan (Ghanaian) word sankofa — “go back and fetch it,” symbolized by a bird looking backward — has been adopted across the African American cultural community as a touchstone for knowing one’s history and honoring ancestors in order to move forward. It appears on Black cultural institutions, in HBCU graduation regalia, in Black bookstores, and in everyday discourse about heritage.

The ancestors

Honoring those who came before — particularly the enslaved generations whose labor and survival made the present possible — is a quietly central practice. “The ancestors are watching” or “do it for the ancestors” invokes their moral presence. Pouring libations — a small amount of water, juice, or alcohol on the ground while naming ancestors — is observed at weddings, funerals, Kwanzaa, and other significant events. Visiting historic Black sites (Tuskegee, Selma, the cotton fields of the Black Belt, the African Burial Ground in New York, the Whitney Plantation, the National Museum of African American History and Culture) is a contemporary form of pilgrimage.

Joy as resistance

Black joy — celebration, pleasure, laughter, dance, beauty, and play — is increasingly named as resistance. To be joyful as a Black person in a society that has tried for centuries to make Blackness synonymous with suffering is itself a political act. The cookout, the family reunion, the wedding, the homecoming, the praise dance, Saturday morning music — all are expressions of joy as resistance.

The Talk

The conversation Black parents have with their children, particularly Black boys, about how to interact safely with police is a tragic and central cultural ritual. Every Black American parent has some version of it: keep your hands visible; do not run; do not reach for your wallet; address officers as Officer and Sir/Ma’am; do not argue; comply first, complain later; come home alive. That the Talk is universal is itself a commentary on the racialized texture of American life.

The cookout

Cultural shorthand for Black community gathering and inclusion. To be “invited to the cookout” means to be accepted as a welcome guest in Black social life. Because of Them We Can: whether Labor Day, Memorial Day, or Independence Day, it means a cookout. No gathering is more sacred; there must be a Spades table.

The Black vote

Black Americans are the most politically cohesive racial-ethnic voting bloc in U.S. politics — voting Democratic at rates around 85–95 percent in presidential elections since 1964. That cohesion reflects the Civil Rights Movement and the Voting Rights Act (1965); shared experience of structural racism across class; the strength of Black political institutions — the Black church, the NAACP, the Urban League, the Congressional Black Caucus, the Divine Nine, Black media; and lived political consciousness around policing, housing, education, healthcare, and economic justice.

Pride in Black institutions

Fierce pride in institutions built within and against a hostile society: HBCUs — Howard, Spelman, Morehouse, Hampton, Tuskegee, Fisk, Florida A&M, North Carolina A&T, Xavier, Dillard, and 100-plus others. Black churches, taken up in Religion. The Divine Nine — Alpha Phi Alpha, Alpha Kappa Alpha, Kappa Alpha Psi, Omega Psi Phi, Delta Sigma Theta, Phi Beta Sigma, Zeta Phi Beta, Sigma Gamma Rho, Iota Phi Theta — central to Black professional and political life. Black-owned businesses — barbershops, beauty salons, restaurants, funeral homes, banks, newspapers, radio stations, publishing houses. Black media — Ebony, Jet (historic), Essence, The Root, BET, The Defender, The Amsterdam News, hundreds of Black newspapers, podcasts, YouTube channels. The NAACP (1909), the National Urban League (1910), SCLC (1957), Black Lives Matter (2013), the Movement for Black Lives.

Somali names often do not match first-middle-last. A common pattern is given name, father’s name, grandfather’s name. There may be no “family surname” as the database understands it. Women do not necessarily take a husband’s name.

What the form invents

The form that demands a last name will invent one. That invented name then follows the person through MHCP, child welfare, and school. It is a gate.

Islamic names are common (Mohamed, Ahmed, Fatima, Amina, Abdi, Hassan). So are Somali names (Hodan, Waris, Degmo, and many others). Pronounce them. Ask. A shortened name for your convenience is a closed door.

Three people in one household may not share a “last name” the way a Swedish Minnesota form expects. That is a naming system. It is not fraud until you have a reason.

targetLesson.title: The Secret War, 1975, and the Camps — Foundational Event

blocks.body:
If the Great Migration is the foundational demographic event of modern Black America, and 1991 of Somali Minnesota, the Secret War and 1975 are the foundational event of Hmong Minnesota.

The Secret War

From 1961 to 1975 the United States, through the CIA, recruited Hmong forces under General Vang Pao to fight in Laos — a war the Geneva Accords had said should not be there. Hmong soldiers blocked supply lines and died in large numbers. Boys were recruited. When the United States left in 1975, the Pathet Lao and Vietnamese forces treated Hmong allied families as the enemy.

Airlift, walk, camps

May 12–14, 1975: airlift from Long Tieng. About 2,500 people in those days. General Vang Pao left May 14. Minnesota later marked that date. Most people were not on the planes. They walked. Thai camps followed — Ban Vinai among the named ones. Years. Then resettlement.

Minnesota

The first Hmong family in Minnesota, Dang Her and Shoua Moua, arrived in December 1975. Church and voluntary-agency sponsors (Lutheran, Catholic, and others) placed people across the country so no one state would “take too many.” Clan and secondary migration undid the scatter. St. Paul became a hub because people chose each other.

U.S. policy at first treated Hmong people as “too primitive” for asylum. The Indochina Migration and Refugee Assistance Act had to be amended. That sentence is literacy for the meeting. It is not a speech you give the family.

blocks.body:
This brief is a language door. Arabic sits on the CLAS ten-language block and the fifteen-language interpreter cards at this department. It is not an Arab module. It is not a Muslim module. If you open Somali Minnesota because Arabic is on the card, you have already closed the door.

Who this is

Arabic is a first language in Lebanese, Iraqi, Syrian, Palestinian, Egyptian, Sudanese, Yemeni, Gulf, and Maghrebi households in this state. It is a liturgical and religious language in some Somali, Oromo, and other Muslim households — recitation, not the interview. Ask which language this family needs. Confirm whether Arabic is actually spoken at home.

Who this is not

There is no dated total “Arab Minnesota” population on this page. Do not invent one. Minnesota Compass (ACS 2019–2023) puts Lebanese Minnesota near 6,959 — one stream, not the whole door. Star Tribune (31 July 2025, citing ACS 2017–2021): Arabic is about 2 percent of Minnesotans who speak a language other than English at home, grouped with German, French, Chinese, and Russian. Date the number you use. A language share is not a people-count.

How to read this

Christian and Muslim Arabs both live here. Lebanese Christian streams are real and older in some Minnesota families. Do not assume mosque. Do not assume hijab. Druze: no dated Minnesota count — do not invent one. If this family is Druze, defer.

Always defer to the person in front of you. This page is a hypothesis you still test on this family.
blocks.heading: A Note on This Guide

blocks.body:
Arabic is an Afro-Asiatic language with a written standard (Modern Standard Arabic / fuṣḥā) and many spoken varieties that are not interchangeable in an interpreter. The language spread with trade, empire, and Islam — and it was already in the Levant and Egypt before that sentence. This is literacy for the desk. It is not a speech you give the family.

History for the meeting

Peoples who use Arabic as a first language do not share one origin story. A Lebanese Maronite household, an Iraqi Chaldean household, a Palestinian family, an Egyptian Copt, a Sudanese Muslim family, a Yemeni household, a Maghrebi household — share a language family and do not share a Tuesday.

What people brought

Do not found “the Arabs” in a waiver meeting. Do not lecture a Christian family about the Prophet. Do not file a Black Sudanese or Nubian Arabic speaker under a Levantine picture. Shared language is not shared culture.

What people brought: a dialect, a church or a mosque or neither, kinship, and a memory of states and wars that are not one war. What they met in Minnesota: an English form, one “Arabic interpreter,” and often a Somali default because the building already has that page.
blocks.heading: Origins — a language, not a people

blocks.body:
The Arabic-speaking world is not one flag and not one race. Levant (Lebanon, Syria, Palestine, Jordan), Egypt, Iraq, Sudan and the Nile, the Maghreb, the Gulf, Yemen. Each has dialects, churches, mosques, and class that do not travel as a blob.

Homeland

In the United States, Dearborn and the Detroit metro, southern California, New York, New Jersey, and Texas hold large communities. Minnesota is not Dearborn. Do not import a Michigan picture onto a Ramsey County lobby.

Minnesota

In Minnesota: Twin Cities and Greater Minnesota both. Compass Lebanese: 81 percent Twin Cities, 19 percent Greater Minnesota (ACS 2019–2023). Other Arabic-speaking streams are not in that profile. Do not assume Minneapolis. Do not assume the person in front of you has been to the country on the passport copy.

blocks.body:
If the Great Migration is the foundational demographic event of modern Black America, and 1991 of Somali Minnesota, 1992–1995 is the foundational event of Bosnian Minnesota.

Foundational events

Yugoslavia broke. Bosnia and Herzegovina declared independence. War followed: siege of Sarajevo, ethnic cleansing, camps, mass rape as a method of war, and on 11 July 1995 the genocide at Srebrenica — more than 8,000 Bosniak men and boys killed after a UN “safe area” failed. That is public record (ICTY, International Court of Justice). It is literacy for the desk. It is not a speech you give the family. Do not ask a survivor to narrate the pit.

Who you meet

Dayton, December 1995, stopped the shooting and froze a political map. Camps and temporary protection in Europe came first for many. U.S. resettlement followed in the mid and late 1990s. Minnesota’s primary-refugee arrivals between 1993 and 2003 were more than 2,300. Secondary migration after that is real and not a Compass cell.

The desk in 2026 does not only meet that first wave. It meets their children — U.S.-born, English-dominant with peers, still translating for a parent who will not tell the war to a stranger and still cannot get the right language in the lobby. If you only know “refugee,” you will miss them.

blocks.body:
This brief is about Burmese Minnesota as a people-page and as a warning about an umbrella. CLAS fifteen interpreter cards say Burmese. Minnesota Compass (ACS 2019–2023) says Burmese 17,123. Both are operations and a U.S. administrative name. They are not a people.

Who this is

Not Karen as a synonym. Not Chin as a synonym. Not Kachin, not Mon, not Rohingya, not “Asian.” Compass Burmese can include Bamar — the majority people of Myanmar, often called Burman — and may overlap or sit beside Chin, Kachin, Rohingya, Mon, Karen. Compass methodology: the Census recodes some people who write Karen into Burmese, with nothing left to show the original response. Ask the people. If the household is Karen, open Karen Minnesota and put S’gaw or Pwo on the line. If Chin, book Chin — Hakha, Falam, or the variety they name. If Rohingya, Rohingya or Bengali may be the language. Burmese is not the default.

Who this is not

Compass, dated: Twin Cities 79.9 percent, Greater Minnesota 20.1 percent. Age 17 or younger 41.5 percent; 65+ 4.2 percent. Foreign-born 67.1 percent. Language other than English (age 5+) 89.6 percent. English less than “very well” 67.0 percent — a severe language gate. High school or higher among 25+ 32.8 percent; bachelor’s or higher 11.8 percent. Median household about $75,513. Poverty 29.6 percent. Owner-occupied 59.0 percent. Average household size 4.99. Disability 12.9 percent. Date Compass. A rate is not the person.

The diversity inside the umbrella is the point. A Bamar Buddhist elder who reads Myanmar script, a Hakha Chin Christian plant worker in Worthington, a S’gaw Karen household that should have opened the Karen page, a Rohingya family who should not have been booked Burmese, a U.S.-born teenager who uses English with friends and still translates a 67-percent-LEP parent — share a country checkbox and do not share a Tuesday.

How to read this

Always defer to the person in front of you. This page is a hypothesis you still test on this family.

blocks.body:
Bamar peoplehood on the Irrawaddy is older than the British and older than the junta. Theravada Buddhism, Burmese as a tonal language with its own script, wet-rice agriculture, and a sequence of kingdoms organized a majority that is not the whole country. Chin, Kachin, Karen, Karenni, Mon, Rakhine, Rohingya, Shan, and others are peoples, not dialects. The country checkbox that says Burma or Myanmar is already a mash.

History for the meeting

British colonial rule, independence in 1948, and decades of military government produced the file this desk meets. 1988. 2007. 2017 in Rakhine. 2021 coup — current structure. Camps in Thailand and Bangladesh are not a personality. They are years of interrupted school, interrupted care, and a kinship the form cannot see.

What people brought

What people brought: language (maybe Burmese, maybe not), church or monastery or mosque, large household, farming and plant skill, a memory of being hunted by a state. What they met in Minnesota: an English form, one “Asian” checkbox, and often one interpreter labeled Burmese for a household that is Chin or Karen.

Homeland

The U.S. map is not only Minnesota: Indiana, New York, Texas, California, and others hold Burma-origin communities. Minnesota is a real resettlement and secondary-migration state, including Greater Minnesota.

Minnesota

Worthington, Albert Lea, Austin, Marshall, and Willmar are a Karen/Burmese pattern in public telling (MSP Magazine on Minnesota’s refugee history names those towns for Karen). Do not assume St. Paul. Do not assume the person in front of you has been to Yangon. A Worthington household is not a Minneapolis default.

Unvarnished, because Minnesota Nice is how a room that treats everyone the same deletes facts.

Named harms

Intergenerational trauma and PTSD sit in this community’s U.S. health literature. Under-identified mental health is a pattern in some rooms. Do not invent a rate. Do not skip screening. Do not make 1975–79 a personality.

Some 1.5-generation gang history in U.S. cities is HISTORY. A last name is not a gang file. Do not score a child on a cousin’s decade.

Deportation of Cambodians with certain convictions — including people who have lived here since childhood — is current structure. It changes who opens the door. Do not collect status you do not need. Do not treat fear as noncompliance.

LGBTQ Khmer Minnesotans exist. You use the name. You do not out someone to kin and call it culture.

Staff who share this community may add facts. They do not get to delete a fact because it is hard to say.

A parent who reads Chinese and limited English is not illiterate. Traditional versus simplified is a real print choice. Many elders read one and not the other. Second generation may not read characters at all. The English-only form is the gate.

Do not skip the interpreter because the last Chinese family was a graduate student. Model-minority as a school story hides the child who is not thriving, the 14.0 percent with less than high school, and the 29.2 percent LEP. CLAS: do not use minors.
blocks.heading: Education

blocks.body:
Elders first. Accept a little food if offered. Shoes off in some homes. Follow this room. Do not perform a drama of respect you saw online.

In the home

Do not photograph an ancestral altar. Do not touch ritual objects. Do not ask an elder to explain Qingming as entertainment. Adoptee households may run on Minnesota Lutheran or Catholic manners — shoes on, first names, a casserole. That is culture too. Do not correct it toward a Beijing script.

Time

Keep medical and legal time. Courtesy-yes then no-show happens when the plan was never agreed. Ask whether they agree. Confirm in the language they use. Mr. or Ms. plus family name until invited is safer with elders.

Do not use a child as the go-between and call it family values. Book the interpreter.

A long answer may be story. A short English yes may be exhaustion or courtesy. Do not take a smile as consent. Ask whether they agree with the plan.

targetLesson.title: Work, Conflict, and Later Streams — Not a Mexican File

blocks.body:
Colombian Minnesota is not an IRCA file and not a 1975 poster. Professional and family streams; internal displacement as a named Colombian fact (desplazados); later asylum and, for some, Temporary Protected Status as a possible U.S. path — pattern now, not a Minnesota count. Do not invent a TPS number. Do not collect status you do not need.

Foundational events

Armed conflict — guerrilla, paramilitary, state, 2016 peace, later violence in some regions — is literacy for the desk. It is not a speech you give the family. It is not every household. The U.S. drug war sat on top of that stack and still sits in a lobby joke. You do not make the joke.

Who you meet

The desk in 2026 meets U.S.-born children, mixed-status households, a professional who does not need an interpreter and whose elder does, and a person who will not put a relative’s name on a form. Compass foreign-born 41.5 percent (ACS 2019–2023) — dated, not a personality.

If you only know “immigrant” or only know “cartel,” you will miss them.

targetLesson.title: 1959, Mariel, 1994, Later — Not One Exile Story

blocks.body:
If 1975 is the foundational event of Vietnamese Minnesota, Cuban Minnesota does not get one year that covers the lobby. It gets a stack, and you will misread the room if you pick the wrong one.

Foundational events

1959–early 1960s: revolution, first-wave exile — often more connected, more already professional. That is a stream, not a virtue ranking. Freedom Flights. Mariel 1980 — a different class mix, a stigma that still sits in some rooms. 1994 balseros. Wet foot/dry foot ended January 2017. Later irregular arrivals via other countries. U.S.-born children in every stream.

Who you meet

Cuban Adjustment Act (1966) is literacy for the desk: a path some people can use after a year of presence. It is not a speech. It is not permission to collect status you do not need. It is not Puerto Rican citizenship.

The desk in 2026 meets a third-generation English-dominant adult, an elder who needs Caribbean Spanish, and last year’s arrival. Compass foreign-born 21.9 percent (ACS 2019–2023) is the dated share — not “everyone is an exile.” 1959 is literacy. It is not a speech you give the family.
